analysis.one_liner: Bans drug manufacturer rebates to insurers and pharmacy benefit managers unless discounts go to patients at the pharmacy counter.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate health committee after being referred in March 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop drugmakers from paying rebates to health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), the middlemen who negotiate drug coverage for employers and insurers. Rebates could only be paid if the discount showed up immediately in what the patient pays at the pharmacy. Any other payment to a PBM would have to be a transparent, flat service fee that the insurer can see. The bill was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay coinsurance based on a drug's list price — people whose out-of-pocket share is calculated off inflated sticker prices — would see discounts applied right at the counter instead of being hidden in rebate deals. Employers and insurers buying coverage would also be able to see exactly what PBMs are paid.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying high drug out-of-pocket costs

how_it_helps.text: Requires that any manufacturer price reduction be reflected at the point of sale, so enrollees get the discount directly at the pharmacy instead of through rebates that lower plan costs behind the scenes [S2].

Bars insurers and their PBM contractors from accepting other remuneration from drugmakers unless it is a flat, transparent service fee with conditions set by the Secretary, including that fees be visible to the health plan [S2].
The rules would have taken effect January 1, 2020 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: PBMs would lose a revenue stream built on negotiated manufacturer rebates, and drugmakers and insurers would have to restructure pricing and contracting. Patients whose premiums are currently subsidized by rebate dollars — typically people who use few prescriptions — could see plans reprice in ways that shift some cost toward premiums.

drawbacks.text: Rebates are discounts plans use to lower premiums for everyone; moving those savings to the pharmacy counter helps heavy drug users but can leave people who fill few prescriptions paying more in premiums than they save [S3].
The bill does not directly lower drug list prices, and drugmakers could keep sticker prices high while paying flat PBM fees instead, so the effect on total national drug spending is uncertain [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of Americans whose out-of-pocket drug costs are computed off list prices, this is a real consumer-protection fix: it stops middlemen and insurers from pocketing discounts patients never see. The tradeoff is genuine but manageable — premiums are partly funded by rebates today, so some low-usage enrollees could pay more in premiums than they save at the counter. It is a narrowly drawn transparency bill, not a comprehensive drug pricing solution.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate health committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun introduced the bill in the Senate on March 5, 2019 [S1].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill's only recorded actions are introduction and committee referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PBMs and the insurers that share in rebate revenue came out ahead: the existing rebate system, where manufacturer discounts flow through middlemen rather than to patients, stayed intact because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PBMs and insurers kept the rebate system

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require point-of-sale pass-through of drug rebates and transparent PBM fees.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after it was referred, so it never reached the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a Republican sponsor and one Republican cosponsor; no committee or floor vote ever recorded a position for or against.

industries.note: PBMs profit by negotiating manufacturer rebates and keeping part of the spread; the bill would let them keep only transparent flat fees. Their gain comes at the cost of patients paying coinsurance off inflated list prices.
Insurers and group health plans receive manufacturer rebates today, often using them to offset premiums; the bill would bar that unless discounts reach enrollees at the point of sale.
Manufacturers would stop paying large rebate pools and instead pay flat service fees, and could keep list prices high; patients would see discounts at the counter but sticker prices would not fall.
